reason: The word has a single sense in the New Testament (rendering religious service to a deity), but the run splits it between "serve" and "worship" with no consistent principle. With a dative object it is "serve" in Acts 24:14, Acts 27:23, Romans 1:9 and 2 Timothy 1:3, but "worship" in Acts 7:42, Hebrews 9:14 and Hebrews 12:28. Two translator notes argue in opposite directions (Acts 24:14 defends "serve", Hebrews 9:14 defends "worship").
sense: to render religious service or devotion to a deity, whether by cultic rites or by a life of devotion; never used of service to human beings

alternates.when: When the verb is used absolutely, with no dative object, for carrying out acts of devotion (Luke 2:37; Acts 26:7; Philippians 3:3). Also when "serve" is already used in the same sentence for δουλεύω and the two must be kept apart (Acts 7:7).
When the participle stands as a noun for the person who performs the rites, with no object (Hebrews 9:9; 10:2).

rationale: In the Septuagint and the New Testament this verb means service given to a god, covering both ritual acts and a whole life of devotion; it is distinct from the verb for bowing in homage (προσκυνέω), which is the word properly rendered "worship". "Serve" keeps the two apart where they stand side by side (Matthew 4:10; Luke 4:8; Romans 1:25) and is the traditional rendering. English "serve" needs an object, so where the Greek has none, "worship" or "worshipper" is the natural equivalent.
standard_view: Standard lexicons define the word as serving in the sense of carrying out religious duties, especially cultic ones. The KJV mostly has "serve", with "worship" in a few places (for example Acts 7:42; 24:14; Philippians 3:3). Modern versions such as the NRSV, ESV and NIV mix "serve" and "worship" by context, usually with "worship" in Acts 24:14, Philippians 3:3 and Hebrews 9:9, 10:2 and 12:28, and "serve" in Matthew 4:10, Romans 1:9 and Hebrews 9:14. The default here is more consistent than most versions but within the range they use.
